claim: Variation in IT population response magnitude can largely account for how well images will be remembered.
source: By analyzing data collected from IT as monkeys performed a visual memory task, we demonstrate that variation in a complementary coding scheme, the magnitude of the population response, can largely account for how well images will be remembered.
evidence: The abstract states this as a main finding based on analysis of neural data from monkeys performing a memory task.

claim: Different natural images evoke different magnitude responses from CNNs trained to categorize objects.
source: We found that, like the brain, different natural images evoked different magnitude responses from these networks
evidence: The abstract reports findings from CNN model analysis.

claim: In higher layers of CNNs, larger magnitude responses are correlated with images that humans and monkeys find most memorable.
source: in higher layers, larger magnitude responses were correlated with the images that humans and monkeys find most memorable.
evidence: The abstract reports correlation findings from CNN analysis.

claim: Variation in IT population response magnitude is a natural consequence of optimizations required for visual processing.
source: Together, these results suggest that variation in IT population response magnitude is a natural consequence of the optimizations required for visual processing, and that this variation has consequences for visual memory.
evidence: The abstract presents this as an inference from the combined neural and CNN results.

claim: At higher stages of visual processing such as inferotemporal cortex (IT), representations of image and object identity are thought to be encoded as distinct patterns of spikes across the IT population.
source: At higher stages of visual processing such as inferotemporal cortex (IT), representations of image and object identity are thought to be encoded as distinct patterns of spikes across the IT population, consistent with neurons that are individually 'tuned' for distinct image and object properties.
evidence: This is stated as established understanding in the field, referencing prior knowledge.

claim: Information about object identity in IT is formatted such that it can be accessed via a weighted linear decoder.
source: information about object identity is formatted such that it can be accessed from IT neural responses via a weighted linear decoder (Figure 1a; reviewed by DiCarlo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article and reference to Figure 1a.

claim: The magnitude of the IT population response is often assumed to be unimportant.
source: The magnitude of the IT population response is often assumed to be unimportant (but see Chang and Tsao, 2017), and it is typically disregarded in population-based approaches, including population decoding and representational similarity analyses (Kriegeskorte et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as a common assumption in the field, with citations to support the claim.

claim: Some images are easy to remember while others are easy to forget.
source: 'Image memorability' refers to the simple notion that some images are easy to remember while others are easy to forget (Isola et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as a definition with citation support.

claim: A large component of image memorability variation is consistent across different individuals.
source: While a large component of image memorability variation is consistent across different individuals (Isola et al., 2011; Khosla et al., 2015), a full account of the sources of image memorability has remained elusive.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Neural correlates of memorability are likely to reside at higher stages of the visual form processing pathway.
source: The neural correlates of memorability are likely to reside at higher stages of the visual form processing pathway, where image memorability can be decoded from human fMRI activity patterns (Bainbridge et al., 2017; Bainbridge and Rissman, 2018), as well as with a consistent cortical timescale from human MEG data at ~150 msec (Mohsenzadeh et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to fMRI and MEG studies.

claim: More memorable images evoke larger fMRI responses.
source: Here we present an alternative proposal, hinted at by the fact that more memorable images evoke larger fMRI responses (Bainbridge et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citation to an fMRI study.

claim: The correlation between image memorability and IT population response magnitudes was strong and highly significant (r = 0.68; p=1×10−15).
source: Figure 2b shows the correlation between image memorability and IT population response magnitudes, which was strong and highly significant (Pearson correlation: r = 0.68; p=1×10−15).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The correlation between memorability and IT response magnitude remained strong when parsed by data from each monkey individually.
source: This correlation remained strong when parsed by the data collected from each monkey individually (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is supported by reference to supplementary figure showing individual monkey data.

claim: The correlation between memorability and IT response magnitude remained strong across the entire 400 ms viewing period after accounting for signal propagation time to IT.
source: and, after accounting for the time required for signals to reach IT, across the entire 400 ms viewing period (Figure 2—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This is supported by reference to supplementary figure showing temporal analysis.

claim: The correlation between memorability and IT response magnitude remained strong when computed for grand mean firing rate.
source: The correlation also remained strong when computed for a quantity closely related to response magnitude, grand mean firing rate (Figure 2—figure supplement 3b)
evidence: This is supported by reference to supplementary figure showing alternative analysis.

claim: The correlation between memorability and IT response magnitude remained strong when the highest firing units were excluded from the analysis.
source: as well as when the highest firing units were excluded from the analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 3c).
evidence: This is supported by reference to supplementary figure showing control analysis.

claim: A strong correlation between memorability and IT response magnitude was observed when images containing faces and/or bodies were excluded (r = 0.62; p=2×10−10).
source: A strong correlation was also observed when images containing faces and/or bodies were excluded from the analysis (Pearson correlation: r = 0.62; p=2×10−10)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from a control analysis.

claim: The results are not an artifactual consequence of recording from patches of neurons enriched for face or body selectivity.
source: suggesting that our results are not an artifactual consequence of recording from patches of neurons enriched for face or body selectivity (Pinsk et al., 2005; Tsao et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an inference from the control analysis excluding face/body images, with citations to prior work on face/body patches.

claim: IT neural responses exhibited repetition suppression for familiar as compared to novel image presentations with a mean proportional reduction of 6.2% in the spike count window.
source: Finally, at the same time that IT neural responses exhibited repetition suppression for familiar as compared to novel image presentations (mean proportional reduction in this spike count window = 6.2%; see also Meyer and Rust, 2018)
evidence: This is a direct report of data analysis with citation to prior work.

claim: The correlation between memorability and IT response magnitude remained strong when computed for novel images (r = 0.62; p=2×10−12).
source: the correlation remained strong when computed for the images both when they were novel (Pearson correlation: r = 0.62; p=2×10−12)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results.

claim: The correlation between memorability and IT response magnitude remained strong when computed for familiar images (r = 0.58; p=8×10−11).
source: as well as when they were familiar (Pearson correlation: r = 0.58; p=8×10−11).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results.

claim: Human-based memorability scores were predictive of the images that monkeys found most memorable during the single-exposure visual memory task.
source: However, our data did allow us to evaluate whether human-based memorability scores were predictive of the images that the monkeys found most memorable during the single-exposure visual memory task, and we found that this was in fact the case (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a direct report of analysis results shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The correlation between image memorability scores and population response magnitudes was significantly higher in trained CNNs compared to randomly initialized versions in all layers.
source: We found that the correlation between image memorability scores and their corresponding population response magnitudes was significantly higher in the trained as compared to a randomly initialized version of the network in all layers
evidence: This is a direct report of CNN analysis results.

claim: The strength of correlation between memorability and CNN response magnitude generally increased across the hierarchy of the network.
source: and the strength of this correlation generally increased across the hierarchy (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a direct report of CNN analysis results shown in Figure 3.

claim: The correlation pattern between memorability and response magnitude was replicated in two other CNNs trained for object classification (AlexNet and VGG-16).
source: These results were also replicated in two other CNNs trained for object classification (Krizhevsky et al., 2012; Simonyan and Zisserman, 2015), where correlation strength also generally increased across the hierarchy of the network (Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is a direct report of replication analysis with citations to the CNN architectures.

claim: The memorability-response magnitude signature is not unique to a particular CNN architecture or training procedure.
source: suggesting that this signature is not unique to this particular architecture or training procedure.
evidence: This is an inference from the replication across multiple CNN architectures.

claim: Variation in population response magnitude across images is reflected in visual systems that are trained to classify objects.
source: These results suggest that variation in population response magnitude across images is reflected in visual systems that are trained to classify objects, and that this variation is directly related to variation in image memorability.
evidence: This is an inference from the CNN analysis results.

claim: Variation in IT population response magnitude has important behavioral consequences for how well images will be remembered.
source: Here we demonstrate that variation in IT population response magnitude has important behavioral consequences for one higher cognitive process: how well images will be remembered.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding based on the combined neural and behavioral data.

claim: Memorability is reflected in IT via a representational scheme that lies largely orthogonal to the one IT uses for encoding object identity.
source: Here we have demonstrated that variation in the ability of humans and monkeys to remember images is strongly correlated with the magnitude of the population response in IT cortex. These results indicate that memorability is reflected in IT via a representational scheme that lies largely orthogonal to the one IT has been presumed to use for encoding object identity (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an inference from the data showing memorability correlates with response magnitude while identity is encoded in response direction.

claim: Representational similarity analysis typically normalizes population response vector magnitude to be the same for all images.
source: For example, investigations of how monkey IT and its human analogs represent objects using 'representational similarity analysis' typically begin by normalizing population response vector magnitude to be the same for all images such that all that is left is the direction of the population response pattern, under the assumption that population vector magnitude is irrelevant for encoding object or image identity (Kriegeskorte et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as a common practice in the field with citation support.

claim: There is variation in the robustness of visual representations within the class of natural images that is not accounted for by classic population-based decoding approaches.
source: The significance of our result follows from the unexpected finding that there is variation in the robustness of visual representations within the class of natural images that is not accounted for by classic population-based decoding approaches, and that this variation correlates with our understanding of the content that makes images more or less memorable.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding and its significance.

claim: Changes in image content can result in IT population response magnitudes that differ by approximately 20%.
source: Our results demonstrate that despite the host of homeostatic mechanisms that contribute to maintaining constant global firing rates across a cortical population (Turrigiano, 2012), changes in image content can result in IT population response magnitudes that differ by ~20% (Figure 2b; Figure 2—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This is a direct report of data analysis with reference to figures and citation to homeostatic mechanisms.

claim: Subsequent memory effects show that indicators of higher neural activity during memory encoding are predictive of more robust remembering later on.
source: Our work relates to 'subsequent memory effects' whereby indicators of higher neural activity in structures both within and outside the medial temporal lobe during memory encoding are predictive of more robust remembering later on (reviewed by Paller and Wagner, 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to a review.

claim: CNNs trained for object recognition mimic many aspects of how IT represents visual object identity.
source: While this class of models has been demonstrated to mimic many aspects of how IT represents visual object identity (reviewed by Yamins and DiCarlo, 2016)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to a review.

claim: CNNs trained for object recognition mimic the neural representation of visual memorability despite not being trained for this task.
source: The fact that CNNs trained for object recognition mimic the neural representation of a distinct behavior – visual memorability – is compelling evidence that this strategy of multiplexing visual identity and memorability results from the computational requirements of optimizing for robust object representations.
evidence: This is an inference from the CNN analysis results.

claim: There is a correlation between VGG-16 CNN responses and patterns of confusions during human rapid visual categorization behavior.
source: Our results are remarkably well-aligned with one study reporting the correlation between one CNN that we tested, VGG-16 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b), and patterns of confusions during human rapid visual categorization behavior (Eberhardt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work and reference to a figure.

claim: There are similarities in object representations between humans and monkeys.
source: However, understanding that memorability variation emerges in CNNs trained for object categorization (Figure 3), coupled with the similarities in object representations between humans and monkeys (Rajalingham et al., 2015), provides insight into the preservation of memorability correlations across these two primate species.
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: A relation between memorability and eye movement patterns exists.
source: The mechanism that we describe here is also likely to be partially but not entirely overlapping with descriptions of salience, where a relation between memorability and eye movement patterns exists (Bylinskii et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: CNNs trained to categorize objects have been coupled with human fMRI responses to predict eye movement behavior.
source: and CNNs trained to categorize objects have been coupled with human fMRI responses to predict eye movement behavior (O'Connell and Chun, 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: Memorability effects are typically found even after controlling for factors commonly associated with salience.
source: However, memorability effects are typically found even after controlling for factors commonly associated with salience, including images features and object categories (Bainbridge et al., 2017; Bainbridge et al., 2013; Mohsenzadeh et al., 2019), suggesting that memorability and salience are unlikely to be one and the same.
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Differences in memorability exist between face stimuli that are identical in saliency in terms of their shapes, parts, image features, and fixation patterns.
source: For example, (Bainbridge et al., 2017; Bainbridge et al., 2013) reported differences in memorability between face stimuli that were identical in saliency in terms of their shapes, parts, image features, and fixation patterns.
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Memorability variation is unlikely to follow primarily from attentional mechanisms that require top-down processing or plasticity beyond that required for wiring up a system to identify objects.
source: The fact that variations in response magnitudes that correlate with memorability emerge from static, feed-forward, and fixed networks suggests that memorability variation is unlikely to follow primarily from the types of attentional mechanisms that require top-down processing or plasticity beyond that required for wiring up a system to identify objects.
evidence: This is an inference from the CNN modeling results showing memorability emerges in feedforward networks.

claim: Neural data were recorded from IT as two rhesus monkeys performed a single-exposure visual memory task.
source: The neural data, also reported in Meyer and Rust (2018), were recorded from IT as two rhesus monkeys performed a single-exposure visual memory task in which they reported whether images were novel (never before seen) or were familiar (seen once previously; Figure 2a).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental methods.

claim: Neural populations with an average size of 26 units were recorded across 27 sessions in total.
source: In each experimental session, neural populations with an average size of 26 units were recorded, across 27 sessions in total.
evidence: This is a direct description of the data collection.

claim: Data were concatenated across sessions into a larger pseudopopulation in a manner that aligned images with similar memorability scores.
source: Because accurate estimate of population response magnitude requires many hundreds of units, data were concatenated across sessions into a larger pseudopopulation in a manner that aligned images with similar memorability scores (see Methods and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis method.

claim: The resulting pseudopopulation contained the responses of 707 IT units to 107 images.
source: The resulting pseudopopulation contained the responses of 707 IT units to 107 images, averaged across novel and familiar presentations.
evidence: This is a direct description of the final dataset.

claim: Experiments were performed on two naïve adult male rhesus macaque monkeys with implanted head posts and recording chambers.
source: Experiments were performed on two naïve adult male rhesus macaque monkeys (Macaca mulatta) with implanted head posts and recording chambers.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental subjects.

claim: All procedures were performed in accordance with the guidelines of the University of Pennsylvania Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.
source: All procedures were performed in accordance with the guidelines of the University of Pennsylvania Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.
evidence: This is a statement of ethical compliance.

claim: Images were never presented more than twice during the entire training and testing period of the experiment.
source: Images were never presented more than twice (once as novel and then as familiar) during the entire training and testing period of the experiment.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental protocol.

claim: The probability of a trial containing a novel vs. familiar image quickly converged to 50% for each class.
source: The probability of a trial containing a novel vs. familiar image quickly converged to 50% for each class.
evidence: This is a direct description of the task design.

claim: Delays between novel and familiar presentations were pseudorandomly selected from a uniform distribution in powers of two (n-back = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64 trials).
source: Delays between novel and familiar presentations were pseudorandomly selected from a uniform distribution, in powers of two (n-back = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64 trials corresponding to mean delays of 4.5 s, 9 s, 18 s, 36 s, 1.2 min, 2.4 min, and 4.8 min, respectively).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental design.

claim: Only 19% of the images used in these experiments contained faces and/or body parts.
source: Only 19% of the images used in these experiments contained faces and/or body parts.
evidence: This is a direct report of image content analysis.

claim: The region of IT recorded was located on the ventral surface of the brain, over an area that spanned 5 mm lateral to the anterior middle temporal sulcus and 14–17 mm anterior to the ear canals.
source: The region of IT recorded was located on the ventral surface of the brain, over an area that spanned 5 mm lateral to the anterior middle temporal sulcus and 14–17 mm anterior to the ear canals.
evidence: This is a direct description of the recording location.

claim: Neural activity was recorded with 24-channel U-probes with linearly arranged recording sites spaced with 100 μm intervals.
source: Neural activity was recorded with 24-channel U-probes (Plexon, Inc) with linearly arranged recording sites spaced with 100 μm intervals.
evidence: This is a direct description of the recording equipment.

claim: The resulting data set included 15 sessions for monkey 1 (n = 403 candidate units) and 12 sessions for monkey 2 (n = 396 candidate units).
source: The resulting data set included 15 sessions for monkey 1 (n = 403 candidate units), and 12 sessions for monkey 2 (n = 396 candidate units).
evidence: This is a direct description of the final dataset after quality control.

claim: Units were screened for stimulus-evoked activity via a comparison of responses before versus after stimulus onset with a two-sided t-test (p<0.01), yielding 353 units for monkey 1 and 354 units for monkey 2.
source: Finally, units were screened for stimulus-evoked activity via a comparison of their responses in a 200 ms period before stimulus onset (−200 ms – 0 ms) versus after stimulus onset (80–280 ms) with a two-sided t-test, p<0.01. This yielded 353 (of 403) units for monkey 1 and 354 (out of 396) units for monkey 2.
evidence: This is a direct description of the data screening procedure and results.

claim: The average standard deviation across the set of memorability scores used to produce each pseudopopulation response was 0.05.
source: The average standard deviation across the set of memorability scores used to produce each pseudopopulation response was 0.05, where memorability ranges 0–1.
evidence: This is a direct report of data quality metric.

claim: MemNet is a CNN trained to estimate image memorability on a large-scale dataset of natural images (LaMem).
source: We obtained memorability scores for the images used in the monkey experiments using MemNet (Khosla et al., 2015) estimates. MemNet is a convolutional neural network (CNN) trained to estimate image memorability on a large-scale dataset of natural images (LaMem; Khosla et al., 2015), publicly available at memorability.csail.mit.edu).
evidence: This is a direct description of the method used to obtain memorability scores.

claim: LaMem consists of 60K images drawn from a diverse range of sources.
source: LaMem consists of 60K images drawn from a diverse range of sources (see Khosla et al., 2015 for more detail).
evidence: This is a direct description of the dataset with citation.

claim: Each image in LaMem is associated with a memorability score based on human performances in an online memory game on Amazon's Mechanical Turk.
source: Each image in this dataset is associated with a memorability score based on human performances in an online memory game on Amazon's Mechanical Turk.
evidence: This is a direct description of how memorability scores were obtained.

claim: MemNet estimates reach 0.64 rank correlation with mean human-estimated memorability.
source: After training, MemNet estimates visual memorability of natural images near the upper bound imposed by human performance: MemNet estimates reach 0.64 rank correlation with mean human-estimated memorability
evidence: This is a direct report of model performance.

claim: The upper bound of consistency between human memorability scores has a rank correlation of 0.68.
source: while the upper bound of consistency between human scores has a rank correlation of 0.68.
evidence: This is a direct report of human performance consistency.

claim: All reported CNN models were evaluated on the full test set of split 1 of LaMem, which contains 10,000 images.
source: All reported models were evaluated on the full test set of split 1 of LaMem, which contains 10,000 images.
evidence: This is a direct description of the evaluation dataset.

claim: HybridCNN is a network with an identical architecture to AlexNet.
source: HybridCNN is a network with an identical architecture to AlexNet (Krizhevsky et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a direct description of the network architecture with citation.

claim: HybridCNN was first trained to classify natural images using data from ImageNet ILSVRC 2012 and Places datasets for a combined 1183-way classification task.
source: HybridCNN was first trained to classify natural images of objects and scenes using data from the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge (ILSVRC) 2012, a 1000-way object classification dataset (Deng et al., 2009), as well as the Places 183-way scene classification dataset (Zhou et al., 2014), for a combined 1183-way classification task.
evidence: This is a direct description of the training procedure with citations.

claim: 95% confidence intervals for the correlation coefficient of each CNN layer were obtained by bootstrapping over 10,000 samples.
source: 95% confidence intervals for the correlation coefficient of each layer were obtained by bootstrapping over the set of 10,000 per-image layer magnitudes and memorability scores. 95% confidence intervals were estimated empirically as the upper and lower 97.5%-centiles of the bootstrapped correlation coefficients for each layer and condition. Bootstrapped resampling was performed independently for each layer and each condition (trained or randomly connected). In all cases, bootstrap estimates were performed using 10,000 samples (with replacement) of the full dataset of 10,000 images.
evidence: This is a direct description of the statistical analysis method.
